See the advanced setup for building a bridge with its own TipTap extension. extendEditorInstance receives the same five arguments as in 1.0, plus an optional sixth context argument (type BridgeContext). It gives your bridge the same message queue the built-in bridges use, so commands sent before the editor is ready aren't lost: import { BridgeExtension } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; type MyMessage = { type: string; payload?: unknown }; type MyEditorInstance = { myCommand: () => void; myQuery: () => Promise<string>; }; declare module '@10play/tentap-editor' { interface EditorBridge extends MyEditorInstance {} } export const MyBridge = new BridgeExtension<{}, MyEditorInstance, MyMessage>({ forceName: 'myBridge', extendEditorInstance: ( sendBridgeMessage, _webviewRef, _editorState, _setEditorState, _platform, context ) => ({ myCommand: () => sendBridgeMessage({ type: 'my-command' }), myQuery: () => context ? context.rpc<string>({ type: 'my-query' }) : Promise.reject(new Error('Needs @10play/tentap-editor 1.1')), }), }); context.rpc adds a messageId to the message payload and resolves with the content of the first reply whose payload.messageId matches, so the web side of your bridge answers with sendMessageBack({ type: 'my-query-back', payload: { content, messageId } }). context.supports(capability) tells you whether the editor bundle in the WebView supports a feature, which is useful when your app may run against a custom bundle built with an older version. The 1.1 web editor advertises 'insertContent', 'selectedText', 'parseOptions', 'styles', 'containerHeight', 'setDynamicHeight' and 'inputMode'; a bundle built with 1.0 or older advertises none. Until the editor is ready, supports returns false. rpc takes an optional second argument: with { capability } it rejects with TentapUnsupportedError when the bundle lacks that capability (this is how getSelectedText handles older bundles), and timeoutMs, which overrides rpcTimeoutMs for that call. The BridgeContext, RpcOptions, SendOptions, Capabilities and CapabilityName types are exported from @10play/tentap-editor.

The BridgeState is the latest state of the editor webview on the native side, it's extendable by BridgeExtensions and is generally used with useBridgeState The list below is the interface of BridgeState in case you use TenTapStarterkit or using all the BridgeExtensions the lib exports, on each prop we specify what bridgeExtension adds it

editable​ boolean Is the editor editable or not extended by CoreBridge empty​ boolean Is the editor empty or not extended by CoreBridge selection​ { from: number; to: number } The selection on the editor-web. from and to are ProseMirror document positions, not character offsets: every block boundary adds a position, so they don't index into the string from getText(). To read the selected text use getSelectedText. extended by CoreBridge isFocused​ boolean true when the editor is focused extended by CoreBridge isReady​ boolean true when the editor is fully loaded and can receive commands. It becomes true as soon as the web editor is created, whether or not it is editable or focused, and goes back to false while the WebView reloads (for example after the system kills its content process). You don't have to wait for it before calling editor methods: commands sent earlier are queued. extended by CoreBridge isBlockquoteActive​ boolean true when the cursor is where blockquote is active a react hook to subscribe to changes on the BridgeState. It takes the EditorBridge and returns the latest BridgeState, re-rendering when it changes. const editorState = useBridgeState(editor); <Button title={editorState.isBoldActive ? 'Unbold' : 'Bold'} onPress={() => editor.toggleBold()} disabled={!editorState.canToggleBold} />; Before the editor is ready the core fields already have values (isReady: false, isFocused: false, empty: true, selection: { from: 0, to: 0 }, and editable from the option), so reading them never throws.

a components that wraps the webview that renders the editor props: name type default description editor EditorBridge The bridge instance that created with useEditorBridge exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage boolean true When true, if you pass an onMessage prop (webview) this will override tentap's own onMessage property. You probably want to disable this, it's here for compatibility. editor must come from useEditorBridge; RichText throws an error for anything else. A spread copy such as { ...editor } is still connected to the same WebView, but prefer passing editor itself. you can also override any of the regular WebView props although this is not recommended

With the default exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage={true}, passing onMessage turns off tentap's own message handling: the editor state, dynamicHeight and onChange stop updating. Pass exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage={false} to receive every message while tentap keeps working: <RichText editor={editor} exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage={false} onMessage={(event) => { const message = JSON.parse(event.nativeEvent.data); if (message.type === 'document-height') { console.log('content height', message.payload); } }} /> A warning is logged in development when onMessage is passed without exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage. Messages may carry extra fields (such as editorId) besides type and payload; ignore the ones you don't use.

style replaces the editor's own WebView styles (including theme.webview), as in 1.0. containerStyle replaces theme.webviewContainer, as in 1.0. Set mergeStyles to merge both on top of the defaults instead. With dynamicHeight, the content height is always applied last, so a flex: 1 or height in your styles doesn't override it. A maxHeight is respected.

Rendering a different editor in the same RichText mounts a new WebView for it. If the WebView's content process is killed by the system, RichText reloads it and restores the editor: queued commands, the last content set with setContent (or the last value read by useEditorContent), injected CSS and settings such as setEditable and setPlaceholder are re-sent, and pending getHTML-style requests are retried. Edits made since that content was last read can be lost in this case.

A react component of a basic Toolbar that include these features: Add link context Change headling context A lot of pre made toolbar items: link quote code bold italic checkList underline strikethrough h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 orderedList bulletList sync lift undo redo props: name type default description editor EditorBridge The bridge instance that created with useEditorBridge hidden boolean a prop to control if toolbar shown. When not set, the toolbar is shown while the editor is focused and a keyboard (system or custom) is up. items ToolbarItem[] DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS array of ToolbarItem's that will be shown on the toolbar headingItems ToolbarItem[] HEADING_ITEMS array of ToolbarItem's shown in the heading context (after pressing Aa) shouldHideDisabledToolbarItems boolean false Indicates whether disabled items should be hidden. Applies to both items and headingItems. ListComponent ComponentType<FlatListProps<ToolbarItem>> FlatList The list that renders the main and heading toolbars, for example a FlatList from a bottom-sheet library. Not used on web. Each toolbar context (main, link, heading) renders its own list, so the heading toolbar always opens scrolled to the start.

HEADING_ITEMS and ToolbarContext are exported, so you can build on the defaults. The first item of HEADING_ITEMS is the close button that goes back to the main toolbar: import { Toolbar, HEADING_ITEMS } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; <Toolbar editor={editor} headingItems={HEADING_ITEMS.slice(0, 4)} />; // close + H1-H3 If you write your own list, include an item that calls setToolbarContext(ToolbarContext.Main) so users can get back to the main toolbar.

Pressing the link item opens the link bar. The link is inserted with the Insert button or the keyboard's Done key, and the link bar stays open when the input loses focus. The input's placeholder (default Type your URL here...) is set with the toolbar.linkBarTheme.hintText key of the theme. tip If the editor or the toolbar is inside a ScrollView, FlatList or KeyboardAwareScrollView, set keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled" on it. Otherwise the first tap on a toolbar button only dismisses the keyboard.

The item rendered by the toolbar component export interface ToolbarItem { onPress: ({ editor, editorState }: ArgsToolbarCB) => () => void; active: ({ editor, editorState }: ArgsToolbarCB) => boolean; disabled: ({ editor, editorState }: ArgsToolbarCB) => boolean; image: ({ editor, editorState }: ArgsToolbarCB) => any; // Accessibility label, read by screen readers and UI test tools label?: string; } type ArgsToolbarCB = { editor: EditorBridge; editorState: BridgeState; setToolbarContext: ( context: ToolbarContext | ((prev: ToolbarContext) => ToolbarContext) ) => void; toolbarContext: ToolbarContext; }; See how we add a custom toolbar item in the color keyboard example
CustomKeyboard, ColorKeyboard and EditorKeyboardAvoidingView are documented in Custom Keyboard Utils.

The useEditorContent hook is designed to efficiently retrieve the content. It monitors changes to the editor's content, and reduces unnecessary data exchanges between web and native, optimizing performance and minimizing message traffic. editor​ EditorBridge (required)
type​ EditorContentType default: 'html' The type of content to return, html and text return strings, json returns an object. debounceInterval​ number default: 10

const content = useEditorContent(editor, { type: 'html' }); useEffect(() => { // Will render each time content is updated and call onSave content && onSave(content); }, [content]); Internally useEditorContent will get the content by calling editor.getHTML (or text/json depending on the type option). To reduce traffic it is called within a debounce with a default interval of 10ms. This can be modified changing the debounceInterval option. The content is fetched once when the editor is ready and then again only when the content changes, not when the selection moves. If responses arrive out of order, an older one never overwrites a newer one, and nothing is fetched after the component unmounts. In addition we can also get the content as text or as a json. If you display the HTML outside the editor, for example with react-native-render-html, see Rendering editor HTML.

A custom keyboard replaces the system keyboard with a React Native view, such as a color picker or a sticker panel, while the editor stays focused. In this page we will show the APIs of the custom keyboard utils. For examples please see: Create custom keyboard or Using the ColorKeyboard

The keyboard is an ordinary view rendered by CustomKeyboard in your own React tree, so it has access to your context providers, state and navigation, and it re-renders like any other component. When it opens, the system keyboard is hidden natively while the editor's WebView keeps focus, so the caret, the selection, a hardware keyboard and IME composition all survive switching between the system and the custom keyboard. Switching is done by a driver: Native driver (default): uses the TenTapKeyboard native module that ships with the package. Needs a native rebuild after installing. Fallback driver: JavaScript only. Used automatically when the native module isn't available (Expo Go, web, a build without the module), when the editor is inside a Modal on Android, and when the native driver fails its self-check. It hides the system keyboard with inputmode="none" on the editor. See limitations.

A react component that renders the active custom keyboard. Render it under your toolbar, as the last child of the same bottom EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, or with layout="overlay" after it (see Layouts). In development on iOS, a warning is logged if the inline keyboard doesn't end at the bottom of the window. keyboards​ CustomKeyboardExtension[] list of CustomKeyboardExtension's activeKeyboardID​ string | undefined the id of the custom keyboard to show. Changing it from an id to undefined closes the custom keyboard and brings the system keyboard back. setActiveKeyboardID​ (id: string | undefined) => void called by CustomKeyboard when the keyboard closes on its own (see closing), so your state stays in sync. Usually the setter of a useState. editor​ EditorBridge the editors EditorBridge instance rootBackground​ ColorValue default: editor.theme.colorKeyboard.keyboardRootColor The background of the area the custom keyboard is drawn in, on both platforms. layout​ 'inline' | 'overlay' default: 'inline' 'inline': CustomKeyboard takes up the keyboard's height in the layout, so a KeyboardAvoidingView around the toolbar and the keyboard keeps the toolbar in place. This is the 0.7.x layout. 'overlay': CustomKeyboard takes no space in the layout and draws the keyboard over the bottom of the screen. Lift your toolbar yourself, with EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, useCustomKeyboardHeight or useKeyboard. Recommended for edge-to-edge apps and for apps using react-native-keyboard-controller. defaultHeight​ number default: 38% of the window height The custom keyboard has the same height as the last system keyboard shown in the current orientation. defaultHeight is used before any system keyboard has been shown. closeOnEditorPress​ boolean default: true Close the custom keyboard and bring back the system keyboard when the user taps the editor. androidKeyboardMode​ 'system' | 'stable' default: 'system' Android only. 'system' never changes your window's softInputMode. With adjustResize the window resizes when the system keyboard hides, which can shift the toolbar for about a frame during the switch. 'stable' sets adjustNothing on the activity window while CustomKeyboard is mounted (API 30+, restored on unmount), so the switch has no shift. Other inputs on the same screen are then no longer resized for; use EditorKeyboardAvoidingView or KeyboardAvoidingView for them. Ignored below API 30 and inside a Modal. Edge-to-edge apps don't need 'stable': their window never resizes. forceFallback​ boolean default: false Always use the JavaScript fallback driver, even when the native module is available. onOpen​ (id: string) => void Called when a custom keyboard has finished opening, with its id. onClose​ () => void Called when the custom keyboard has finished closing. onKeyboardError​ (event: KeyboardErrorEvent) => void interface KeyboardErrorEvent { reason: 'verify-timeout' | 'native-error'; driver: 'native' | 'fallback' | 'inline'; error?: unknown; } 'verify-timeout': the system keyboard was still up 600 ms after the driver tried to hide it. If the native driver failed, CustomKeyboard switches to the fallback driver for as long as it stays mounted. If the fallback failed too, the custom keyboard closes and the system keyboard stays. 'native-error': the native module threw; error holds what it threw. A warning is also logged in development. onKeyboardHideAndroid​ () => void Deprecated, use onClose. Kept from 0.7.x. Called on both platforms when the system keyboard comes back while a custom keyboard is up. rootRef​ React.RefObject<any> Deprecated, ignored. Needed by the iOS keyboard in 0.7.x. You can remove it.

A class that defines a custom keyboard. const StickerKeyboard = new CustomKeyboardExtension( 'keyboard.sticker', StickerKeyboardComp, { height: 280 } // optional ); id​ string a unique key for the custom keyboard comp​ ComponentType The custom keyboard component. It is rendered inside your app like any other component and receives: prop type description editor EditorBridge the editor the keyboard belongs to close () => void closes the custom keyboard and brings back the system keyboard keyboardHeight number the height the keyboard is drawn at The props type is exported as CustomKeyboardComponentProps. Components written for 0.7.x that take no props keep working. options.height​ number optional A fixed height in dp for this keyboard, instead of following the system keyboard's height. The constructor still registers the component with AppRegistry under id, as in 0.7.x. tentap no longer uses that registration.

A ready-made CustomKeyboardExtension (id keyboard.color) with text color and highlight buttons. Picking a color applies it and focuses the editor, which returns to the system keyboard. Colors and styles come from the colorKeyboard theme. See the ColorKeyboard example.

const { activeKeyboardID, open, close, dismiss } = useCustomKeyboard(); // or useCustomKeyboard(editor) A hook to control the custom keyboard from your own components, such as a toolbar button or the keyboard itself. It can be called anywhere, not only inside CustomKeyboard. It controls: the CustomKeyboard of editor, when you pass one; otherwise, the CustomKeyboard rendering the component that calls it (inside a keyboard component); otherwise, the most recently mounted CustomKeyboard. When there is no matching CustomKeyboard, activeKeyboardID is undefined and the functions do nothing. open and close go through the same transitions as changing activeKeyboardID, and setActiveKeyboardID is called so your state follows. field type description activeKeyboardID string | undefined the open custom keyboard open (id: string) => void opens a custom keyboard. Switching from one custom keyboard to another just swaps the content. close (toSystem?: boolean) => void closes the custom keyboard. With toSystem (default true) the system keyboard comes back; with false both are dismissed. dismiss () => void same as close(false)

const height = useCustomKeyboardHeight(); // or useCustomKeyboardHeight(editor) The height of the open custom keyboard, or 0. Use it with layout="overlay" to add space under your toolbar or content, for example when another library already handles the system keyboard. It reads the CustomKeyboard of editor, or the most recently mounted one.

A view that adds bottom padding equal to the part of it whichever keyboard covers, system or custom, so the toolbar at its bottom sits fully on top of the keyboard. It measures where it ends in the window and compares that with the top of the keyboard (useKeyboard().keyboardTop), so it needs no keyboardVerticalOffset below a navigation header or above a tab bar, it covers the navigation bar an edge-to-edge Android keyboard reaches over (also without the native module, as in Expo Go), and it adds nothing where the window already resized for the keyboard (Android adjustResize without edge-to-edge). Unlike React Native's KeyboardAvoidingView it keeps the same padding while switching between the two keyboards, so the toolbar doesn't move. An inline CustomKeyboard inside it takes its own space, so the padding leaves that out. Place it around the editor and the toolbar (for example inside a SafeAreaView with edges={['top']}), and put the Toolbar in a row so its default flex: 1 doesn't share the column with the editor: <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1 }} edges={['top']}> <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}> <View style={{ flex: 1 }}> <RichText editor={editor} /> </View> <View style={{ flexDirection: 'row' }}> <Toolbar editor={editor} /> </View> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView> <CustomKeyboard layout="overlay" {...keyboardProps} /> </SafeAreaView> Props: all View props, plus prop type default description keyboardVerticalOffset number 0 distance in dp between the bottom of this view and the bottom of the window, subtracted from the padding until the view was measured. Not needed otherwise enabled boolean true false removes the padding

Marks a view that is drawn on top of the keyboard, such as your own toolbar, so that RichText keeps the line being typed about one line above it. The library's Toolbar does this itself. Pass false while the view is hidden. const MyToolbar = ({ editor }: { editor: EditorBridge }) => { const { isKeyboardUp } = useKeyboard(); const accessory = useKeyboardAccessory(isKeyboardUp); return <View onLayout={accessory.onLayout}>{/* buttons */}</View>; }; Views that start above the editor (a static toolbar at the top of the screen) are ignored. A toolbar that is not marked still gets the default toolbar height of room when the editor reaches behind the keyboard, but marking it keeps the margin exact.

A dynamicHeight editor is as tall as its content and does not scroll itself, so inside a ScrollView the line being typed can grow under the keyboard. useScrollToCaret scrolls the ScrollView to keep the caret about one line clear of the keyboard, the toolbar on it and the ScrollView's edges: const EditorInScrollView = () => { const editor = useEditorBridge({ dynamicHeight: true }); const scrollViewRef = useRef<ScrollView>(null); useScrollToCaret(editor, scrollViewRef); return ( <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}> <ScrollView ref={scrollViewRef} keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"> <RichText editor={editor} /> </ScrollView> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView> ); }; It needs the web bundle of this version (custom bundles built before 1.1 do not report the caret).

const { isKeyboardUp, keyboardHeight, isCustomKeyboardOpen, activeCustomKeyboardID, systemKeyboardHeight, lastKeyboardHeight, } = useKeyboard(); field description isKeyboardUp true while the system keyboard or a custom keyboard is up keyboardHeight height of whichever keyboard is up. It doesn't drop to 0 while switching between the system and a custom keyboard. isCustomKeyboardOpen true while a custom keyboard is open activeCustomKeyboardID id of the open custom keyboard systemKeyboardHeight height of the system keyboard, 0 while it is hidden lastKeyboardHeight the last usable system keyboard height, kept after it hides; 0 before the first one windowOverlaysKeyboard true when the keyboard covers the window instead of resizing it: iOS, Android edge-to-edge or 'stable' mode keyboardCoverHeight how far up from the bottom of the window the keyboard reaches: its height plus, on edge-to-edge Android, the navigation bar it also covers. 0 when no keyboard covers the window, including a system keyboard the window resizes for inlineKeyboardHeight height of the slot an open inline CustomKeyboard takes in the layout, 0 for an overlay keyboard or none keyboardTop top of whichever keyboard is up in window coordinates (the space of measureInWindow), or null. A view whose bottom is viewBottom in the window is covered by Math.max(0, viewBottom - keyboardTop). A custom keyboard takes the place of the system keyboard Its type is exported as KeyboardState. isKeyboardUp and keyboardHeight behave as in 1.0 when no custom keyboard is used. Heights are in dp.
Deprecated. The native view used by the 0.7.x keyboard. It now renders nothing and logs a warning in development; remove it from your code.

The custom keyboard closes, and setActiveKeyboardID(undefined) is called, when: the user taps the editor (unless closeOnEditorPress={false}): the system keyboard comes back you call editor.focus(): the system keyboard comes back activeKeyboardID is set to undefined, or close() from useCustomKeyboard is called the editor loses focus, or another input opens the system keyboard the Android back button is pressed: both keyboards are dismissed the editor's WebView reloads When CustomKeyboard unmounts, the system keyboard suppression is undone, but setActiveKeyboardID is not called.

CustomKeyboardProps, CustomKeyboardComponentProps, CustomKeyboardExtensionOptions, AnyCustomKeyboardExtension, CustomKeyboardControls (the return type of useCustomKeyboard), EditorKeyboardAvoidingViewProps, AndroidKeyboardMode, KeyboardErrorEvent, KeyboardPhase, KeyboardDriverKind, KeyboardState and TenTapViewProps are exported from @10play/tentap-editor.

Android Modal: an editor inside a React Native Modal uses the fallback driver, because the modal is a separate window. Fallback driver on iOS: while a custom keyboard is open, the globe key on a hardware keyboard doesn't work. Fallback driver on Android: on Android System WebView older than 66, tapping the editor brings back the system keyboard, which closes the custom keyboard. Web: the custom keyboard renders inline under the toolbar; the browser's keyboard isn't hidden. Floating, split and Stage Manager keyboards on iPad are not mirrored: the custom keyboard uses the docked keyboard height.

a react hook that will return EditorBridge The returned editor keeps the same reference for the lifetime of the component, so it is safe to use in dependency arrays. Pass that object to RichText. A spread copy such as { ...editor } also works, but its option fields are a snapshot taken when it was made. bridgeExtensions​ BridgeExtension[] default: TenTapStartKit A list of BridgeExtensions that will be added to the editor on the native side. Extensions with the same name are deduplicated and the last one wins, so spread TenTapStartKit first and put your configured bridges after it. Bridges are read when the editor is created. Adding a bridge to the list after mount has no effect (a warning is logged in development); remount the editor instead. initialContent​ string | object default: undefined initial content that will be loaded first on the editor. A string is parsed as HTML, an object as TipTap JSON. parseOptions​ { preserveWhitespace?: boolean | 'full'; from?: number; to?: number; topOpen?: boolean } default: undefined The serializable subset of ProseMirror parse options used when HTML is parsed: for initialContent, for insertContent and for every setContent call that doesn't pass its own. It is read when the editor loads. By default ProseMirror collapses runs of whitespace in HTML to a single space. Use preserveWhitespace: 'full' to keep them: const editor = useEditorBridge({ initialContent: "hello world", parseOptions: { preserveWhitespace: 'full' }, }); With 'full', newlines and indentation between tags in pretty-printed HTML also become content. If you round-trip content saved from the editor, storing it with getJSON() keeps whitespace exactly with no parse options. note parseOptions needs the 1.1 web editor. If you use a custom editor bundle, rebuild it after upgrading. autofocus​ boolean default: false when true the editor focuses at the end of its content when it becomes ready. It runs once per load, so it also refocuses after the WebView reloads. avoidIosKeyboard​ boolean default: false This helps keep the cursor visible above the keyboard when the editor is full-screen and the virtual keyboard hides the bottom portion of the editor. While the keyboard is up, RichText measures how far the keyboard and the views drawn on it (the Toolbar, or your own toolbar marked with useKeyboardAccessory) reach into the editor, and then: Adds that much bottom padding to the document, plus about one line Sets ProseMirror's scroll threshold and margin to the same value, so the line being typed stays about one line above the toolbar Scrolls the cursor back into view when the keyboard or toolbar moves over it Removes the padding when the keyboard is dismissed This works the same for the system keyboard and an open custom keyboard, on iOS and Android, edge-to-edge or not, and wherever the editor ends: behind the keyboard, above a KeyboardAvoidingView, or inside one that already avoids the keyboard (where only the one-line margin is added). It is skipped when dynamicHeight is on, because the WebView is already only as tall as its content; see useScrollToCaret for an editor that grows inside a ScrollView. The measured inset applies to every editor, so an editor covered by the keyboard keeps its cursor visible even without this option. An editor that ends above the keyboard still keeps the line being typed about one line above its own bottom edge. If the editor reaches behind the keyboard and no view on the keyboard is marked, RichText assumes a toolbar of your own sits there and keeps the default toolbar height clear too; mark your toolbar with useKeyboardAccessory to measure it exactly. Until the first measurement, an editor with avoidIosKeyboard falls back to the 1.0 behaviour: the keyboard height on iOS (and wherever the keyboard overlays the window), or a fixed toolbar height on Android. avoidKeyboard​ boolean default: false An alias of avoidIosKeyboard with a name that matches what it does. avoidIosKeyboard keeps working and wins when both are set. scrollBottomOffset​ number default: 0 Extra space in px kept between the cursor and the bottom of the editor, on top of what RichText measures for the keyboard and toolbar. It is added to the scroll threshold and to the bottom padding, so new lines scroll into view before they reach something drawn over the editor that RichText cannot measure: const editor = useEditorBridge({ scrollBottomOffset: 60, // e.g. the height of your floating action bar }); The Toolbar, and views marked with useKeyboardAccessory, are already measured while the keyboard is up, so they need no offset. Unlike calling updateScrollThresholdAndMargin yourself, this value is kept when the keyboard opens and closes. With dynamicHeight the padding is part of the content height, so the editor is that much taller than its text. A capped dynamic-height editor needs it to scroll its last line above something drawn over it (#308). Without it, a capped dynamic-height editor keeps about one line between the caret and its own bottom edge when it scrolls. dynamicHeight​ boolean default: false when true the editor's webview keeps the same height as its content. It grows and shrinks with the content in any parent, not only inside a ScrollView. A height cap such as maxHeight on the container is respected. Once the cap is reached the editor scrolls internally and keeps its scroll position. Keyboard padding (avoidIosKeyboard) is not applied in this mode. When the editor grows inside a ScrollView, useScrollToCaret scrolls the ScrollView to keep the line being typed above the keyboard. It can change after mount and the document is kept. A custom editor bundle built with a version before 1.1 keeps the value it loaded with and only the container height changes, as in 1.0. Rebuild the bundle to switch it at runtime. The content height in px is also sent as a document-height message. To read it yourself, pass onMessage to RichText together with exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage={false}. To scroll a long document together with other content, put the editor inside your own ScrollView. See Editor inside a ScrollView. disableColorHighlight​ boolean default: undefined when true the selection highlight will be off and when false will be on, on android this will be off by default, please see: https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/issues/184#issuecomment-2304826219 theme​ EditorTheme default: defaultEditorTheme (light theme) this prop can be used to customize default styles, see theme example editable​ boolean default: true When set to false the editor will be readonly. Changing it after mount calls editor.setEditable. onChange​ () => void A callback that is called each time the editor's content has changed. The content itself is not passed, so that every keystroke doesn't send the whole document from the WebView to React Native. To keep the content in state, use useEditorContent, which is debounced and handles this for you: const editor = useEditorBridge({ initialContent }); const content = useEditorContent(editor, { type: 'html' }); useEffect(() => { if (content !== undefined) save(content); }, [content]); If you prefer onChange, fetch the content inside it with editor.getHTML, editor.getJSON or editor.getText, ideally debounced. The latest onChange is always the one called, so it can close over fresh state. See Working with content. mergeStyles​ boolean default: false By default the style and containerStyle props of RichText replace the editor's own styles (the default WebView styles and theme.webview, and theme.webviewContainer), as in 1.0. When true, your styles are merged on top of them instead. With dynamicHeight the content height is applied in both cases. rpcTimeoutMs​ number default: undefined (no timeout) How long the async methods (getHTML, getText, getJSON, getSelectedText, and requests sent by custom bridges through context.rpc) wait for the WebView before rejecting with a TentapRpcTimeoutError. Without it they wait indefinitely, as in 1.0. The time counts from the call, including any wait for the editor to load and time after the editor unmounted, so requests pending at unmount still reject. The option is read when the editor is created. import { TentapRpcTimeoutError } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; const editor = useEditorBridge({ rpcTimeoutMs: 5000 }); try { const html = await editor.getHTML(); } catch (e) { if (e instanceof TentapRpcTimeoutError) { // the WebView didn't answer in time } } customSource​ string default: SimpleEditorBundleString used in advance setup, an HTML string that will replace the default simple editor webviewBaseURL​ string default: undefined The baseUrl of the WebView's HTML source. Relative URLs in your content and CSS (images, fonts) resolve against it. On iOS, point it at a file:// directory to let the WebView read local files, for example fonts loaded from a file. DEV​ boolean default: false prop used in advance setup, when true the webview will load DEV_SERVER_URL instead of the html string DEV_SERVER_URL​ string default: http://localhost:3000 prop used in advanced setup, a url string that points to the editor dev server

An Interface of all the commands you can do with the editor on the react native side, can be extended with a BridgeExtension. With all of the bridges included in TenTapStartKit the EditorBridge will have the methods below. A method only exists when its bridge is in bridgeExtensions. For example, toggleBold is added by BoldBridge; if you pass your own bridgeExtensions array without it, toggleBold is missing from both the object and its type. Commands can be called right away, even before the editor has loaded. They are queued and sent in order once the editor is ready. focus​ (pos?: 'start' | 'end' | 'all' | number | boolean | null) => void a function that will focus the editor and open the keyboard. If a custom keyboard is open, it closes and the system keyboard comes back. extended by CoreBridge blur​ a function that will blur the editor and close the keyboard extended by CoreBridge webviewRef​ RefObject a ref for the webview that renders the editor extended by CoreBridge getEditorState​ () => BridgeState a function that will return the most up to date BridgeState extended by CoreBridge getHTML​ () => Promise an async function that will return the content of the editor in html format. List items are always wrapped in a paragraph (

  • …

    • ); see Rendering editor HTML if you display the HTML outside the editor. extended by CoreBridge getText​ () => Promise an async function that will return the content of the editor in text format extended by CoreBridge getJSON​ () => Promise

The async methods can reject with these errors, both exported from @10play/tentap-editor: Error When TentapRpcTimeoutError The WebView didn't answer within rpcTimeoutMs. Has requestType and timeoutMs. TentapUnsupportedError The editor bundle doesn't support the method, usually a custom bundle built with an older version. Has capability.

In this example we will configure some extensions. Each bridge comes with the configureExtension function, that configures it's underline tiptap extension. For full list of available configurations for each bridge please see BridgeExtensions.

First we can check which options are available to extend on the tiptap docs. Links to them are available here In our case let's extend the placeholder to show custom text, and the link extension to not open links when clicking them const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: [ ...TenTapStartKit, PlaceholderBridge.configureExtension({ placeholder: 'Type something...', }), LinkBridge.configureExtension({ openOnClick: false }), ], }); Bridges are deduplicated by name and the last one wins, so spread TenTapStartKit first and the configured bridges after it.

We can also extend the main tiptapExtension of each bridge with extendExtension. Let's say we want to update the Document extension of the CoreBridge to mandate a heading as the first node: We could do CoreBridge.extendExtension({ content: 'heading block+' }); Now the Document extension will be configured to have a heading node first followed by one or many "blocks"

In this example we will be creating a basic editor that contains all of the pre-built bridgeExtensions and a toolbar on top of the keyboard. Jump To Full Example

The first thing we want to do is create our EditorBridge. To do this we will use the useEditorBridge hook. This by default will contain the TenTapStartKit which includes all of the following bridge extensions. Now we have added all of the pre-built bridgeExtensions provided by tentap, and our editor will support all of these bridgeExtensions features const editor = useEditorBridge(); This is the same as passing const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: TenTapStartKit, });

Now we will add our RichText component, this is simply a WebView that runs a pre-built tiptap bundle with some extensions, that is then communicated with via our bridgeExtensions The RichText component receives the EditorBridge we created before <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <RichText editor={editor} /> </SafeAreaView>;

Our RichText is pretty empty without a toolbar, so let's add one. We wrap the editor and the toolbar in an EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, which makes room for the keyboard so the toolbar sits right on top of it: <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <RichText editor={editor} /> </View> <View style={exampleStyles.toolbarRow}> <Toolbar editor={editor} /> </View> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView> </SafeAreaView>; EditorKeyboardAvoidingView measures how far the keyboard reaches into it, so it needs no keyboardVerticalOffset below a navigation header and it also works on edge-to-edge Android. The Toolbar shows itself while the editor is focused and the keyboard is up, and the editor keeps the line being typed above it. See Keyboard and caret. The 1.0 version of this example, with React Native's KeyboardAvoidingView absolutely positioned at the bottom of the screen, keeps working. See the 1.0 layout.

import React from 'react'; import { StyleSheet, View } from 'react-native'; import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context'; import { EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, RichText, Toolbar, useEditorBridge, } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; export const Basic = () => { const editor = useEditorBridge({ autofocus: true, avoidIosKeyboard: true, initialContent, }); return ( ); }; const exampleStyles = StyleSheet.create({ fullScreen: { flex: 1, }, toolbarRow: { flexDirection: 'row', }, }); const initialContent = `

This is a basic example!

`; More screens, including custom keyboards, dynamic height and a navigation header, are in the example apps: example/ (React Native CLI) and example-expo/ (Expo dev client).
In this example we will be adding custom css and fonts

Each bridge, gives us the option to configureCSS. Some bridges come with css already configured in them, when we can override by configuring. Let's give an example by overriding the CodeBridge. First let's define the css const customCodeBlockCSS = ` code { background-color: #ffdede; border-radius: 0.25em; border-color: #e45d5d; border-width: 1px; border-style: solid; box-decoration-break: clone; color: #cd4242; font-size: 0.9rem; padding: 0.25em; } `; Now let's configure the CodeBridge to use this css const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: [ // It is important to spread StarterKit BEFORE our extended plugin, // as plugin duplicated will be ignored ...TenTapStartKit, CodeBridge.configureCSS(customCodeBlockCSS), // Custom codeblock css ], }); NOTE calling configureCSS more than once will override the previous css.

Let's say we want to dynamically update css after the editor is initialized. We can do this with injectCSS. injectCSS receives two parameters: css: the css to inject tag: the tag of the stylesheet of which to inject the css into When we call injectCSS it gets or creates a stylesheet with the given tag and updates it's css. If we wanted to update our CodeBridge css after it has been initialized we could run editor.injectCSS(ourCustomCSS, CodeBridge.name); then this would replace or create the existing css with whatever we have given it. Now let's say that we don't want to override a bridges existing css, we could do this by providing a custom tag editor.injectCSS(ourCustomCSS, 'our-custom-tag'); This will create a new stylesheet with our-custom-tag and it will not override any bridge's custom css. injectCSS can be called at any time: calls made before the editor has loaded are queued, and the stylesheet is applied again if the WebView reloads.

There are two ways to load a font into the editor: from a file (recommended), or embedded as base64 in the CSS. In both cases pass the CSS through configureCSS rather than injectCSS, so the font is part of the editor from the first paint.

Loading the font from a local file avoids sending and parsing a large base64 string every time the editor loads. Get a local file URI for the font. With Expo, use expo-asset; in a bare app, copy the font into your app bundle and build the path yourself. Reference it from an @font-face rule and pass the CSS to CoreBridge.configureCSS. Allow the WebView to read local files. On iOS, also set webviewBaseURL to a file:// directory that contains the font. Create the editor only once the URI is known, because bridge CSS is read when the editor is created. import { useAssets } from 'expo-asset'; export const EditorWithFont = () => { const [assets] = useAssets([require('./assets/Rubik-Regular.ttf')]); const fontUri = assets?.[0]?.localUri; if (!fontUri) return null; return <Editor fontUri={fontUri} />; }; const Editor = ({ fontUri }: { fontUri: string }) => { const editor = useEditorBridge({ webviewBaseURL: fontUri.substring(0, fontUri.lastIndexOf('/') + 1), bridgeExtensions: [ ...TenTapStartKit, CoreBridge.configureCSS(` @font-face { font-family: 'Rubik'; src: url('${fontUri}'); } * { font-family: 'Rubik', sans-serif; } `), ], }); return ( <RichText editor={editor} allowFileAccess allowFileAccessFromFileURLs /> ); };

This needs no setup, at the cost of a larger editor HTML that is parsed on every load. So first we need to download and convert our font, so we can inject it into the webview: Upload your font files to https://transfonter.org and check the 'base64' option. When you download the zip file, there will be a stylesheet.css file there. Copy the contents of the stylesheet.css into a new ts file and export it as a string. export const ProtestRiotFont = ` font-family: 'Protest Riot'; src: url('data:font/woff2;charset=utf-8;base64,.......... ....... `; Now we can use our font as follows const customFont = ` ${ProtestRiotFont} * { font-family: 'Protest Riot', sans-serif; } `; And inside our EditorBridge const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: [ // It is important to spread StarterKit BEFORE our extended plugin, // as plugin duplicated will be ignored ...TenTapStartKit, CoreBridge.configureCSS(customFont), // Custom font ], });

The default editor doesn't set a font, so the WebView uses its default serif font. For CJK characters it then falls back to a system font that may have no bold or italic variant, and bold or italic text looks unchanged even though the marks are applied. Set a font stack that has CJK weights and let the WebView synthesize the missing styles: const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: [ ...TenTapStartKit, CoreBridge.configureCSS(` .ProseMirror { font-family: -apple-system, system-ui, 'PingFang SC', 'Hiragino Sans GB', 'Noto Sans CJK SC', 'Microsoft YaHei', sans-serif; font-synthesis: weight style; } `), ], }); The default font is unchanged in 1.x so existing editors look the same.

In this example we will add the ColorKeyboard, and a custom button to toggle it in the Toolbar. The same screen is in example/src/Examples/Keyboard/WithKeyboard.tsx and example-expo/src/screens/CustomKeyboard.tsx.

First we need a state of the current active keyboard id (used inside the toolbar to show and hide the color keyboard) const [activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard] = React.useState<string>(); Then, into an EditorKeyboardAvoidingView at the bottom of the screen we add the CustomKeyboard component, right under the toolbar <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.keyboardAvoidingView}> <Toolbar editor={editor} /> <CustomKeyboard activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard} keyboards={[ColorKeyboard]} // <-- here we add the color keyboard editor={editor} /> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>;

Now that we have added the custom keyboard, we need to add a button to the toolbar so we can open it. We create a new component ToolbarWithColor that adds a button toggling the color keyboard in front of the default items. interface ToolbarWithColorProps { editor: EditorBridge; activeKeyboard: string | undefined; setActiveKeyboard: (id: string | undefined) => void; } const ToolbarWithColor = ({ editor, activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard, }: ToolbarWithColorProps) => { return ( <Toolbar editor={editor} items={[ { onPress: () => () => { const isActive = activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id; if (isActive) editor.focus(); setActiveKeyboard(isActive ? undefined : ColorKeyboard.id); }, active: () => activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id, disabled: () => false, image: () => Images.palette, }, ...DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS, ]} /> ); }; The toolbar stays visible while the color keyboard is open. Picking a color applies it and brings the system keyboard back, and tapping the editor closes the color keyboard too. Then all that is left to replace Toolbar with our new ToolbarWithColor and we're done! <ToolbarWithColor editor={editor} activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard} />

Select some text and pick a color

The colors, their labels and the keyboard's styles come from the colorKeyboard key of the editor theme. See Color keyboard theme.
In this example we will add a custom theme

We can also provide a custom theme useEditorBridge({ theme: { toolbar: { toolbarBody: { borderTopColor: '#C6C6C6B3', borderBottomColor: '#C6C6C6B3', backgroundColor: '#474747', }, // Check the ToolbarTheme type for all options }, webview: { backgroundColor: '#1C1C1E', }, webviewContainer: {}, }, }); The theme you pass is deep-merged into the default theme, so you only need to set the keys you change.

The link bar that opens from the toolbar's link button is styled by toolbar.linkBarTheme. Its hintText key sets the placeholder of the URL input: useEditorBridge({ theme: { toolbar: { linkBarTheme: { hintText: 'Paste a link', placeholderTextColor: '#8E8E93', }, }, }, });

The ColorKeyboard is styled by the colorKeyboard key: useEditorBridge({ theme: { colorKeyboard: { keyboardRootColor: 'white', // background of the keyboard area colorSelection: [ // Custom colors in color keyboard { name: 'Custom Color', value: '#E5112B', displayColor: '#E5112B', // Optional - the color that will be displayed on ui (if left empty will default to use value) }, ], // Check the ColorKeyboardTheme type for all options }, }, }); colorSelection and highlightSelection replace the default lists instead of being merged with them, so the example above shows a single color. colorKeyboard is optional on EditorTheme; when it's missing, the default color keyboard theme is used. darkEditorTheme includes a dark color keyboard theme. The Color and ColorKeyboardTheme types, and the built-in defaultColorKeyboardTheme and darkColorKeyboardTheme, are exported from @10play/tentap-editor, so you can build on the default lists: import { defaultColorKeyboardTheme } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; useEditorBridge({ theme: { colorKeyboard: { colorSelection: [ ...defaultColorKeyboardTheme.colorSelection, { name: 'Brand', value: '#E5112B' }, ], }, }, });

In this example we will implement darkmode in the editor. This is similar to setting up custom css. Dark mode has two parts: the native side (toolbar, link bar, color keyboard, WebView background), styled by the theme option; the web side (the document inside the WebView), styled with CSS.

To use the built-in dark theme on the native side, pass darkEditorTheme: const editor = useEditorBridge({ theme: darkEditorTheme, }); darkEditorTheme includes a dark toolbar and a dark colorKeyboard theme (darkColorKeyboardTheme), so the ColorKeyboard follows too. Now we just need to update the web-side css with configureCSS: import { CoreBridge, darkEditorCss, darkEditorTheme, TenTapStartKit, useEditorBridge, } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; const editor = useEditorBridge({ bridgeExtensions: [ ...TenTapStartKit, CoreBridge.configureCSS(darkEditorCss), // <--- Add our dark mode css ], theme: darkEditorTheme, // <-- Add our dark mode theme });

theme is read on every render, so it can follow useColorScheme(). Bridges, and the CSS configured on them, are read once when the editor is created. To switch the web-side CSS at runtime, inject it with injectCSS under its own tag: import React, { useEffect } from 'react'; import { useColorScheme } from 'react-native'; import { darkEditorCss, darkEditorTheme, defaultEditorTheme, RichText, useEditorBridge, } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; export const ThemedEditor = () => { const dark = useColorScheme() === 'dark'; const editor = useEditorBridge({ theme: dark ? darkEditorTheme : defaultEditorTheme, }); useEffect(() => { // An empty string clears the stylesheet with this tag. editor.injectCSS(dark ? darkEditorCss : '', 'dark-mode'); }, [dark, editor]); return <RichText editor={editor} />; }; injectCSS calls made before the editor has loaded are queued, and the stylesheet is applied again if the WebView reloads. Alternatively, remount the screen with a key when the scheme changes and pick the bridges for that scheme, as the example-expo app does.
To change the colors, pass a partial theme; it is deep-merged into the default theme. See Custom Theme, including the color keyboard theme.

Below a react-navigation header, a KeyboardAvoidingView needs a keyboardVerticalOffset equal to the header height plus the top inset, and that height changes between platforms and OS versions. A hard-coded value leaves the toolbar partly behind the keyboard. EditorKeyboardAvoidingView does not need the offset. documents.t: getHTML() and useEditorContent return the HTML that TipTap produces. When you display it outside the editor, for example in a read-only list with react-native-render-html, a few details of that HTML matter.

In TipTap and ProseMirror a list item always contains a paragraph, so lists come out as:

Web editors hide the paragraph margins with CSS. react-native-render-html gives every

its default vertical margins and doesn't support selectors like li > p, so each list item gets extra space. The editor's output can't change without breaking saved content and nested lists, so remove the margins when rendering. A custom p renderer can drop them only inside list items: import RenderHtml, { type CustomBlockRenderer } from 'react-native-render-html'; const ParagraphRenderer: CustomBlockRenderer = ({ TDefaultRenderer, tnode, style, ...props }) => ( ); const renderers = { p: ParagraphRenderer }; ; If you don't need paragraph spacing anywhere, tagsStyles={{ p: { marginTop: 0, marginBottom: 0 } }} is enough.

Task lists are <ul data-type="taskList"> with <li data-checked="true"> items that contain a <label> with a checkbox and a <div> with the content. Style or replace them the same way if you render them outside the editor.

The editor may add a hidden after an inline node at the end of a line. It is only part of the editor's DOM, not of getHTML(), but if you style images with CSS inside the editor, scope the rules as img:not(.ProseMirror-separator).

The layout above: CustomKeyboard takes up the keyboard's height under the toolbar, and an EditorKeyboardAvoidingView around both keeps the toolbar in place for the system keyboard. This is the 0.7.x layout with EditorKeyboardAvoidingView in place of React Native's KeyboardAvoidingView; the 0.7.x version keeps working where the window resizes for the keyboard.

EditorKeyboardAvoidingView pads its content by the height of whichever keyboard is up and keeps the same padding while switching, so it doesn't depend on the timing of React Native's keyboard events. Combine it with layout="overlay", and render CustomKeyboard after it, outside the padded view: <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen} edges={['top']}> <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}> <RichText editor={editor} /> </View> {/* In a row, the toolbar's default flex: 1 only fills the width */} <View style={{ flexDirection: 'row' }}> <StickerToolbar activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard} editor={editor} /> </View> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView> <CustomKeyboard layout="overlay" activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard} keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]} editor={editor} /> </SafeAreaView> Here the toolbar is part of the layout instead of being absolutely positioned, and the editor shrinks to make room for whichever keyboard is up. This is the recommended layout for edge-to-edge Android apps.

react-native-keyboard-controller only knows about the system keyboard, so its KeyboardAvoidingView and KeyboardStickyView drop to the bottom while a custom keyboard is open. Use layout="overlay" and add the custom keyboard's height yourself with useCustomKeyboardHeight: import { KeyboardStickyView } from 'react-native-keyboard-controller'; import { useCustomKeyboardHeight } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; const ToolbarArea = ({ editor, activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard, }: ToolbarWithStickersProps) => { const customKeyboardHeight = useCustomKeyboardHeight(); return ( <KeyboardStickyView style={{ position: 'absolute', width: '100%', bottom: 0 }} offset={{ closed: -customKeyboardHeight }} > <StickerToolbar editor={editor} activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard} /> </KeyboardStickyView> ); }; // somewhere below, outside the sticky view: <CustomKeyboard layout="overlay" activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard} setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard} keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]} editor={editor} />;

With the default androidKeyboardMode="system" the window keeps your softInputMode. With adjustResize (the React Native default) the window resizes when the system keyboard hides, and the custom keyboard takes its space only once React Native reports the hide. The toolbar drops to the bottom and comes back up while switching to the custom keyboard, and is pushed up briefly while switching back. To avoid it: use the overlay layout, or set androidKeyboardMode="stable" on CustomKeyboard. It switches the window to adjustNothing while CustomKeyboard is mounted (Android 11+), and restores your mode on unmount. It needs the native module, so it has no effect in Expo Go, with the fallback driver or inside a Modal. Other inputs on that screen then need a KeyboardAvoidingView or EditorKeyboardAvoidingView. Edge-to-edge apps (the default with targetSdk 36) are not affected: their window never resizes.

Expo Go can't load the native TenTapKeyboard module, so CustomKeyboard uses the JavaScript fallback driver automatically. No code changes are needed; build a dev client for the native driver. You can also force the fallback with forceFallback to compare the two. The fallback is also used inside a React Native Modal on Android, and when the native driver fails its self-check (reported through onKeyboardError). See the limitations.

onChange tells you that the content changed, without sending the content itself, because sending the whole document from the WebView on every keystroke is expensive. The easiest way to keep the content in state is useEditorContent: const editor = useEditorBridge({ initialContent }); const content = useEditorContent(editor, { type: 'html' }); // or 'text' | 'json' useEffect(() => { if (content !== undefined) saveDraft(content); }, [content]); If you prefer onChange, fetch the content yourself, ideally debounced: const saveLater = useMemo( () => debounce((html: string) => saveDraft(html), 500), [] ); const editor = useEditorBridge({ onChange: async () => { saveLater(await editor.getHTML()); }, }); onChange is called with the latest version of your callback, so it can use fresh state.

TenTap is a typed, easy to use, customizable, and extendable Rich Text editor for React-Native based on Tiptap and Prosemirror. It offers a "plug and play" experience and comes with many essential features out of the box that can be incorporated into your apps quickly. Additionally, TenTap allows you the developers to tailor the editor to your applications specific needs.

💁 Based on tiptap ➕ Extendable ⚙️ Support dynamic scheme 🛠️ Native toolbar 🎹 Custom keyboards 💅 Customizable styles 🌒 Darkmode and custom theme support 🏗️ Supports the new architecture (including bridgeless) and the old architecture See Installation for the supported React Native versions.

After years of developing rich text editors for mobile, we realized that there is an empty void for open source RichText editors on mobile especially for ReactNative. So we have decided to create this package that incorporates all that we have learned, and that provides the best possible ux. Tentap is designed for getting the best experience of editing rich-text on mobile inspired by state of the art mobile editors like: gdocs, notion, dropbox paper.

EditorBridge - a bridge to control the editor from the native side - will be extended by bridgeExtensions bridgeExtension - a typed class that helps us communicate between the native part and the webview part There are two different ways to work with this lib: simple and advanced, simple should be good enough for most of the cases, we tried to make the API as simple as possible so people will be able to plug and play, on the other hand advanced usage requires a longer setup.

With the simple usage you get all the standard rich text abilities as you can get from other libs like: react-native-pell-rich-editor / react-native-cn-quill ordered / bullet / check Lists Bold/Italic/Underline Placeholder Image color/highlight and more... With the simple usage you have all of these bridgeExtensions available. With tentap you can also control the scheme of your editor by passing the useBridgeEditor list of bridgeExtensions you want, so in case you build a chat app and you don't want to let users underline you should not pass the Underline bridgeExtension, that will make sure that even if the user will copy paste some text with underline, when pasted the underline will not be parsed. Custom keyboards - custom keyboards let you swap the system keyboard for a React Native view, for example a color picker or a sticker panel, while the editor keeps its focus, caret and selection. See the color keyboard example and the custom keyboard example.

In case you want to add your own tiptap extension / build your own bridgeExtension you will have to bundle the web editor by your own that way you will get full control of what running inside the webview. In this case we provide utils/components/hooks that can help you customize the editor but still get all the features and exp fixes tentap can offer. See the advanced setup You can also see an example in example/src/Examples/Advanced.

It rebuilds the editor core, fixes a long list of bugs, adds a few options and methods, and brings back custom keyboards. This page lists the upgrade steps, the optional improvements, and what behaves differently.

Update the package (and react-native-webview, if it is older than 13.7): yarn add @10play/tentap-editor@^1.1.0 Rebuild your native app. 1.1 contains a small autolinked native module (TenTapKeyboard), used by custom keyboards. Until you rebuild, the editor works and custom keyboards use the JavaScript fallback driver. iOS: cd ios && pod install Android: a new Gradle build Expo: npx expo prebuild, or rebuild your dev client. Expo Go keeps working without a rebuild. If you use the advanced setup, rebuild your editor bundle and follow Upgrading your editor-web. Coming from 0.x, delete the old editorHtml.ts from your build folder (for example editor-web/build/editorHtml.ts). Since 1.0, buildEditor.js writes editorHtml.js and editorHtml.d.ts instead, and a Vite config with emptyOutDir: false keeps the old file. Metro resolves .ts before .js, so import { editorHtml } from './editor-web/build/editorHtml' would keep loading the 0.x bundle. editor:build prints a warning while such a file exists. Coming from 0.7.x, also follow the 1.0 migration guide. In particular, TipTap v3 renamed History to UndoRedo, so HistoryBridge is named undoRedo; code that looks bridges up by 'history' must use 'undoRedo'. 1.1 also sends the bridge's config under history, so a custom editor bundle built with 0.7.x still receives it.

React Native 0.74 or newer (Expo SDK 51 or newer) for the native module. The Android module is built on BaseReactPackage, which was added in 0.74, so the Android build fails on older versions. The react-native peer dependency is still *, so package managers don't check this. Stay on 1.0.x if you can't upgrade React Native. react-native-webview 13.7 or newer. Use 13.13.3 or newer on the new architecture if the editor is inside a ScrollView. The Android package is still com.tentap.TenTapViewPackage, now written in Java. The library no longer applies the Kotlin Gradle plugin, which conflicted with AGP 9's built-in Kotlin support. package.json declares a codegenConfig again (RNTenTapSpec, a native module). If a build fails on stale codegen output after upgrading, clean the build folders (ios/build, android/app/build) and rebuild. @tiptap/react is still a dependency, so a 1.0 advanced setup that imports EditorContent from @tiptap/react keeps building. Importing it from @10play/tentap-editor instead is recommended (Sharing tiptap). react-dom is no longer installed with the package. 1.0.1 depended on react-dom@^18.2.0, and a React 19 app then got a second, nested react-dom 18, which expo-doctor reports as a duplicate (#315). The built-in editor is prebuilt with its own copy, and the native bundle never loads react-dom. Web apps and custom editor bundles keep a react-dom that matches their react, as in advanced setup. A native-only app needs nothing extra. @tiptap/react still lists react-dom as a peer dependency, so a native-only install may print a peer warning; that warning is safe to ignore.

The 1.0 layout, a KeyboardAvoidingView around the Toolbar with a keyboardVerticalOffset below a header, keeps working. 1.1 adds EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, which needs no offset and also keeps the toolbar on the keyboard on edge-to-edge Android (the default in Expo SDK 53+). Swapping it in is a one-line change; see Keyboard and caret.

CustomKeyboard, ColorKeyboard, CustomKeyboardExtension, the colorKeyboard theme and the Color / ColorKeyboardTheme types are exported again. See Custom Keyboard Utils. Coming from 0.7.x: Your code compiles unchanged. rootRef is ignored and can be removed. The keyboard component is now rendered in your app's own React tree. It can use your context providers and hooks, including useBridgeState(editor) to follow the editor state. It also receives editor, close and keyboardHeight props. It works on the new architecture, including bridgeless mode and the React Native 0.79+ app templates. TenTapView is a deprecated component that renders nothing. Remove it. colorKeyboard is optional on EditorTheme, so a full theme object written for 1.0 still type-checks. editor.theme, defaultEditorTheme and darkEditorTheme are typed with it, so editor.theme.colorKeyboard.keyboardRootColor compiles as in 0.7.x. The toolbar stays visible while a custom keyboard is open, so you can drop the hidden logic from the 0.7.x examples.

parseOptions ProseMirror parse options, e.g. to keep whitespace scrollBottomOffset extra space kept below the cursor avoidKeyboard alias of avoidIosKeyboard mergeStyles merge the RichText style prop instead of replacing rpcTimeoutMs timeout for getHTML and the other async methods insertContent insert HTML, text or JSON at the cursor getSelectedText read the selected text setContent(content, options) parseOptions and emitUpdate per call Toolbar headingItems customize the heading toolbar; HEADING_ITEMS and ToolbarContext are exported TentapRpcTimeoutError, TentapUnsupportedError errors thrown by the async methods useRemoteEditorBridge subscribes to the most recently created editor Toolbar ListComponent render the toolbar with another list component, such as a bottom-sheet FlatList linkBarTheme.hintText placeholder of the link bar input useTenTap stateUpdateDebounceMs debounce of state updates from a custom editor bundle

These are fixes, but they change what some apps observe. Editor identity useEditorBridge returns the same object on every render, so it is safe in dependency arrays; its option fields (theme, dynamicHeight, …) always read the latest render. RichText and Toolbar re-render when the options change, also under a React.memo parent. Your own memoized components that render from editor.theme or another option should take that value as a prop, since editor alone no longer changes. Readiness and messaging isReady becomes true as soon as the editor is created, also when it is not editable and not focused. It goes back to false while the WebView reloads. Commands called before the editor is ready are queued and sent in order once it is ready. They used to be dropped with an "Editor isn't ready yet" warning. The web editor sends editor-ready followed by a full stateUpdate as soon as it is created. If you read messages in your own onMessage: messages can carry extra fields (editorId, v) besides type and payload, editor-ready has a payload, and there are new message types (boot-error, tentap-editor-press). Ignore what you don't use. A development warning is logged when onMessage is passed without exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage; the default is still true. If the WebView's content process is killed, the editor reloads and restores its content and settings. Edits made since the content was last read can be lost. On iOS, the WebView is remounted after its first load only with react-native-webview 13.12.3 and 13.12.4, which need the workaround. useEditorContent fetches the content when it changes, not on every selection change. Bridge configs containing quotes or </script> no longer break the editor. Layout style and containerStyle passed to RichText still replace the editor's own styles, as in 1.0, unless you set the new mergeStyles option. The difference: with dynamicHeight, the content height is now applied after your containerStyle, so your styles can no longer switch dynamic height off by accident. RichText throws a clear error when editor doesn't come from useEditorBridge. A spread copy such as { ...editor } still works, as in 1.0, but its option fields are a snapshot, so prefer passing editor itself. dynamicHeight works in any parent, shrinks when content is deleted, keeps the scroll position when the height is capped, and no longer adds keyboard padding. Keyboard and caret RichText measures how far the keyboard and the toolbar on it reach into the editor, and keeps the line being typed about one line above the toolbar. In 1.0 the inset was derived from the keyboard height (iOS) or a fixed toolbar height (Android), so the caret could end up under the toolbar. The document padding and the scroll threshold now come from this measurement. This applies to every editor without dynamicHeight while a keyboard is up, also without avoidIosKeyboard. An editor that ends above the keyboard keeps about one line of space below the caret. Until the first measurement, avoidIosKeyboard keeps its 1.0 value. A toolbar of your own on the keyboard that isn't marked with useKeyboardAccessory gets the default toolbar height of room. useKeyboard() keeps keyboardHeight while switching between the system and a custom keyboard, and returns new fields. isKeyboardUp and keyboardHeight behave as in 1.0 when no custom keyboard is used. Editing setImage adds an empty paragraph after an image that ends the document and moves the cursor there. Links without a scheme get https:// (www.google.com → https://www.google.com), or the defaultProtocol passed to LinkBridge.configureExtension. Plain email addresses get mailto:. CSS injected with injectCSS is re-applied when the WebView reloads. Toolbar shouldHideDisabledToolbarItems also hides disabled heading items. The link bar no longer closes when its input loses focus. The keyboard's Done key inserts the link. Each toolbar context renders its own list, so the heading toolbar opens scrolled to the start. Advanced setup tiptapOptions.onCreate, onUpdate, onSelectionUpdate and onTransaction passed to useTenTap run in addition to tentap's handlers instead of replacing them. If you overrode them on purpose to stop tentap's messages, that no longer works. Bridges and extensions are resolved once, when the editor is created.

EditorBridge (with CoreBridge) has two new required members, insertContent and getSelectedText. If you build EditorBridge objects by hand, for example as test mocks, add them. setContent has a new optional second parameter. EditorTheme has a new optional colorKeyboard key. The source types are self-contained: deep imports from @10play/tentap-editor/src/... and moduleResolution: "node" no longer report missing bridge methods such as toggleBold. Importing from the package root is still recommended. extendEditorInstance receives an optional sixth argument, BridgeContext. Existing five-argument bridges are unaffected.

Deprecated Use instead CustomKeyboard rootRef prop nothing, it's ignored TenTapView nothing, it renders nothing CustomKeyboard onKeyboardHideAndroid prop onClose Deprecated APIs keep working in 1.x. avoidIosKeyboard is not deprecated; avoidKeyboard is an alias with a clearer name.

yarn add @10play/tentap-editor react-native-webview cd ios && pod install Then rebuild your app (yarn ios / yarn android). The package contains a small native module (TenTapKeyboard) used by custom keyboards. It is autolinked: pod install adds it on iOS and Gradle picks it up on Android, with no changes to your native code. The editor itself doesn't depend on it. If it is missing, for example in a build made before you installed the package, everything keeps working and custom keyboards use a JavaScript fallback driver. After upgrading the package, run pod install again and rebuild, so the native module matches the JavaScript.

npx expo install @10play/tentap-editor react-native-webview Development build / prebuild (recommended): everything works, including the native keyboard driver. No config plugin is needed. Rebuild your development build (npx expo run:ios, npx expo run:android, or EAS) after installing or upgrading. If you commit the native folders, run npx expo prebuild again. Expo Go: the editor works. Expo Go can't load the native module, so custom keyboards use the JavaScript fallback driver automatically (see Expo Go and the fallback driver). Expo Go also ships its own react-native-webview version, so test an editor inside a ScrollView in a development build. The advanced setup also needs a development build. Now you're ready to add tentap to your app! Continue with Keyboard and caret for the screen layout, or jump to the basic example.

Supported React Native JavaScript: any version supported by react-native-webview. Native module: 0.74 or newer, old and new architecture (bridge and bridgeless). Expo SDK 51 or newer for development builds and prebuild. Expo Go is supported with the keyboard fallback. react-native-webview 13.7 or newer. Use 13.13.3 or newer on the new architecture if the editor is inside a ScrollView (see Editor inside a ScrollView). iOS 15.1 or newer (or your app's min_ios_version_supported) Android The library builds with minSdkVersion 24. The editor is tested on Android 10 (API level 29) and newer, which we recommend as your minimum. androidKeyboardMode="stable" needs Android 11 (API level 30). The React Native 0.74 floor is documented here and isn't enforced by the package. The Android native module needs BaseReactPackage (added in React Native 0.74) and doesn't compile on older versions. The peer dependencies (react, react-native, react-native-webview) are all *, as in 1.0, so your package manager won't warn you. Stay on 1.0.x if you can't upgrade React Native. The TipTap packages, @tiptap/react and lodash are regular dependencies and are installed for you. The built-in editor bundle already contains react-dom, and the native app never loads it. If your app targets the web or builds a custom editor bundle, add a react-dom that matches your react to your own package.json.

The repository has two example apps: example/: React Native CLI (React Native 0.81), built on both the new and the old architecture. It has every example in these docs, including the advanced setup. example-expo/: Expo with a development build. It also runs on the web.
For expo-web support follow this guide
Some additional steps are necessary for supporting expo web. The example-expo app in the repository runs on the web with this setup (yarn example:expo web); there is also a standalone example here.

npx expo install @10play/react-native-web-webview react-native-web react-dom expo-crypto expo-crypto and the crypto alias below are only needed by older versions of @10play/react-native-web-webview; the example-expo app runs version 0.0.3 without them. Keeping them does no harm. Several editors on one page work with any version of @10play/react-native-web-webview: the shim delivers every editor's messages to every WebView on the page, so 1.1 tags each message with an editor id and every editor ignores messages meant for another one. A custom onMessage on RichText only receives its own editor's messages too.

Which bundler are you using? Metro Webpack Create config file if not already npx expo customize metro.config.js Into your metro.config.js add the following configuration const { getDefaultConfig } = require('expo/metro-config'); /** @type {import('expo/metro-config').MetroConfig} */ const config = getDefaultConfig(__dirname); const webAliases = { 'react-native': 'react-native-web', 'react-native-webview': '@10play/react-native-web-webview', 'react-native/Libraries/Utilities/codegenNativeComponent': '@10play/react-native-web-webview/shim', 'crypto': 'expo-crypto', }; config.resolver.resolveRequest = ( context, realModuleName, platform, moduleName ) => { if (platform === 'web') { const alias = webAliases[realModuleName]; if (alias) { return { filePath: require.resolve(alias), type: 'sourceFile', }; } } return context.resolveRequest(context, realModuleName, platform, moduleName); }; module.exports = config; Create config file if not already npx expo customize webpack.config.js Into your webpack.config.js add the following configuration const createExpoWebpackConfigAsync = require('@expo/webpack-config'); module.exports = async function (env, argv) { const config = await createExpoWebpackConfigAsync(env, argv); // Alias react-native-webview and crypto config.resolve.alias = { ...config.resolve.alias, 'react-native': 'react-native-web', 'react-native-webview': '@10play/react-native-web-webview', 'crypto': 'expo-crypto', }; // Shim codegenNativeComponent config.resolve.fallback = { ...config.resolve.fallback, 'react-native/Libraries/Utilities/codegenNativeComponent': '@10play/react-native-web-webview/shim', }; return config; };
Restart metro for changes to take effect and the editor should load

dynamicHeight works on web: the height is applied to the iframe's style, which is the only style the shim reads. Custom keyboards render under the toolbar, but the browser's own keyboard isn't hidden on web. They use the JavaScript driver; there is no native module on web. On web the Toolbar renders its items without a FlatList, so ListComponent isn't used.
Make sure you read the core concepts page before setup advance and check if the simple usage is good enough for you. See full working example here https://github.com/10play/10TapAdvancedExample

Create a new folder in your project called editor-web (or any other name) - advance setup will let you full control on what running inside the editor webview, so we need to create a separate folder that will include code that will run inside the webview and will have different build process and tsconfig

Create editor-web/tsconfig.json: editor-web/tsconfig.json { "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/tsconfig", "_version": "2.0.0", "compilerOptions": { "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"], "module": "esnext", "paths": { "@10play/tentap-editor": [ "../node_modules/@10play/tentap-editor/lib-web/typescript/webEditorUtils/index.d.ts" ] }, "moduleResolution": "bundler", "target": "es2015", "allowJs": true, "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true, "esModuleInterop": true, "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true, "isolatedModules": true, "jsx": "react-jsx", "noEmit": true, "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true, "resolveJsonModule": true, "skipLibCheck": true, "strict": true } } It's important to configure paths so on web the web types will be used instead of native types.
Add exclude on the root tsconfig.json: "exclude": ["./editor-web"]

Add the following files index.html RichTextEditor
AdvancedEditor.tsx import React from 'react'; import { EditorContent, useTenTap, TenTapStartKit } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; import { CounterBridge } from '../CounterBridge'; /** * Here we control the web side of our custom editor */ export const AdvancedEditor = () => { const editor = useTenTap({ bridges: [...TenTapStartKit, CounterBridge], }); return ( ); }; index.tsx import React from 'react'; import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; import { AdvancedEditor } from './AdvancedEditor'; /** * This is the entrypoint for the "web" part of our editor that will be built with vite */ declare global { interface Window { contentInjected: boolean | undefined; } } /** * On android - react-native-webview there is a bug where sometimes the content * is injected after the window is loaded https://github.com/react-native-webview/react-native-webview/pull/2960 * To overcome this we will check if the content is injected before rendering the editor */ const contentInjected = () => window.contentInjected; let interval: NodeJS.Timeout; interval = setInterval(() => { if (!contentInjected()) return; // Once content is injected into the webview, we can render the editor const container = document.getElementById('root'); const root = createRoot(container!); root.render(); clearInterval(interval); return; }, 1);
