documents.t: We chose to use vite as our bundler so first run yarn add -D vite @vitejs/plugin-react vite-plugin-singlefile And now let's create vite.config.ts and configure it vite.config.ts import { defineConfig } from 'vite'; import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'; import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile'; // This config is used to build the web editor into a single file export default defineConfig({ root: 'src/editor-web', // This should be the directory of your index.html build: { outDir: 'build', }, resolve: { alias: [ { find: '@10play/tentap-editor', // On our web bundle we only want to include web related code replacement: '@10play/tentap-editor/web', }, // We alias tiptap view and state to use the internal version of tiptap to avoid this error https://github.com/ueberdostiptap/issues/3869#issuecomment-2167931620 { find: '@tiptap/pm/view', replacement: '@10play/tentap-editor/web', }, { find: '@tiptap/pm/state', replacement: '@10play/tentap-editor/web', }, ], }, plugins: [react(), viteSingleFile()], server: { port: 3000, }, }); It's important to have the alias configuration so vite will not load react-native code Sharing tiptap with @10play/tentap-editor/web​ @10play/tentap-editor/web is a prebuilt bundle with its own copy of tiptap and ProseMirror inlined. Code you import from @tiptap/* in your editor-web, such as extra extensions, is bundled separately, and the two copies don't recognize each other's objects. Bundler options such as vite's resolve.dedupe cannot merge them, because the copy inside @10play/tentap-editor/web is not a package in node_modules. Import EditorContent (and useEditor if you need it) from @10play/tentap-editor, not from @tiptap/react, so the editor and the component that renders it come from the same copy. Keep the @tiptap/pm/view and @tiptap/pm/state aliases above, so extensions share ProseMirror's view and state classes with the bundled editor. Install extra @tiptap/* extensions at the same version that @10play/tentap-editor uses (npm ls @tiptap/core shows it).

Add scripts on package.json so it will be easy to run/build editor-web: package.json "scripts": { ... "editor:dev": "vite --config ./editor-web/vite.config.ts", "editor:build": "vite --config ./editor-web/vite.config.ts build && yarn editor:post-build", "editor:post-build":"node ./node_modules/@10play/tentap-editor/scripts/buildEditor.js ./editor-web/build/index.html", "reverse-android": "adb reverse tcp:3000 tcp:3000", } editor:dev - Run the editor web in dev mode editor:build - Build the editor web, probably need to add to your deploy/build process editor:post-build - This will take your built html file and write editorHtml.js (with editorHtml.d.ts), which exports it as the string editorHtml which we can then later use as the source of our RichText. reverse-android - On android need to reverse ports so it will be able to work with DEV / DEV_SERVER_URL props

Outside of editor-web update your EditorBridge to used the html we just built. import { editorHtml } from './editor-web/build/editorHtml'; const editor = useEditorBridge({ customSource: editorHtml, // ...your other options });

yarn add react-dom yarn add -D @types/react-dom Install the react-dom version that matches your react. You basically done with the advance setup now you have full control of the editor-web you can write your own bridgeExtensions add additional tiptapExtensions

useTenTap creates the TipTap editor inside the WebView and connects it to React Native. import { TenTapStartKit, useTenTap } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; import { CounterBridge } from '../CounterBridge'; const editor = useTenTap({ bridges: [...TenTapStartKit, CounterBridge], tiptapOptions: { editorProps: { attributes: { spellcheck: 'false' } }, }, }); bridges: the bridges the editor-web knows about. A bridge with a TipTap extension is enabled when the native side's bridgeExtensions contains a bridge with the same name. A bridge without one, such as a bridge that only adds to the editor state or handles your own messages, always runs. Bridges and extensions are resolved once, when the editor is created. tiptapOptions: options passed to TipTap's useEditor. Its extensions are added after the bridges' extensions, so pass only extensions that none of your bridges adds. CoreBridge (part of TenTapStartKit) already adds Document, Paragraph and Text; passing them again makes TipTap warn about duplicate extension names. The event handlers onUpdate, onSelectionUpdate and onTransaction run after tentap's own handlers instead of replacing them, and onCreate is yours alone (tentap no longer uses it to announce the editor), so none of them can break the connection to React Native. Every other option, such as content, editable, parseOptions, editorProps or shouldRerenderOnTransaction, overrides tentap's default. stateUpdateDebounceMs: how long editor state updates are debounced before they are sent to React Native. default: 10. The first state update after the editor is created is always sent right away. useTenTap returns the TipTap Editor (or null before it exists). Its options type is exported as UseTenTapArgs.

Rebuild your editor bundle (yarn editor:build) whenever you upgrade @10play/tentap-editor. Bundles built with an older version keep working, but miss the newer web-side features: insertContent, getSelectedText, parseOptions, and the dynamic height and readiness fixes. getSelectedText rejects with TentapUnsupportedError on such a bundle. When upgrading from 1.0, also: change #root div.dynamic-height .ProseMirror in your index.html to height: auto; min-height: 0; display: flow-root; as shown above, so dynamic height can shrink, doesn't loop on iOS and includes the first and last paragraph margins (1.1 also injects this rule, so a bundle that wasn't rebuilt yet gets it too); preferably import EditorContent from @10play/tentap-editor instead of @tiptap/react, and follow Sharing tiptap. The contentInjected polling in index.tsx still works. In 1.1 the configuration is written into the customSource HTML before your script runs, so the first check already passes.

info In case you are using Expo you have to use this Alternative Setup for dev mode on your advance setup editor There is an alternative vite setup that does not require a vite dev server as suggested in #80. This setup does not require we add the DEV prop

In vite.config.ts, add a plugin that runs editor:post-build after every build, and set emptyOutDir: false: vite.config.ts import { exec } from 'child_process'; import { defineConfig } from 'vite'; import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'; import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile'; export default defineConfig({ root: 'src/editor-web', build: { outDir: 'build', emptyOutDir: false, }, resolve: { // the same aliases as above }, plugins: [ react(), viteSingleFile(), { name: 'postbuild-commands', closeBundle: async () => { exec('yarn editor:post-build', (error) => { if (error) console.error(`exec error: ${error}`); }); }, }, ], });

Update the editor:dev script to watch the advanced editor instead of running a dev-server, the hot reload will be handled by metro and not vite. "editor:dev": "vite --config ./editor-web/vite.config.ts -w build"

This page shows the screen layout that keeps the toolbar on top of the keyboard and the line being typed above the toolbar, on iOS and Android, with or without a navigation header, on edge-to-edge Android and with custom keyboards.

Wrap the editor and the toolbar in an EditorKeyboardAvoidingView: import React from 'react'; import { StyleSheet, View } from 'react-native'; import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context'; import { EditorKeyboardAvoidingView, RichText, Toolbar, useEditorBridge, } from '@10play/tentap-editor'; export const Editor = () => { const editor = useEditorBridge({ autofocus: true, avoidIosKeyboard: true, initialContent: '

Start editing!

', }); return ( ); }; const styles = StyleSheet.create({ fullScreen: { flex: 1, }, // The toolbar's default flex: 1 would share the column with the editor; // in a row it only fills the width. toolbarRow: { flexDirection: 'row', }, }); EditorKeyboardAvoidingView measures where it ends in the window and pads its bottom by the part of it that the keyboard covers. The editor gets shorter, and the toolbar sits right on the keyboard: No keyboardVerticalOffset. It works below a navigation header, above a tab bar and inside a SafeAreaView, because it measures its real position instead of relying on an offset. Edge-to-edge Android. This is the default in Expo SDK 53+, and for apps targeting SDK 35+ on Android 15+. The keyboard there also covers the navigation bar, and React Native's keyboard height leaves that out. EditorKeyboardAvoidingView measures against the top of the keyboard, so the toolbar isn't partly hidden. This also works without the native module (Expo Go). adjustResize. When the window already shrinks for the keyboard, it adds no padding. Custom keyboards. The padding stays the same while you switch between the system keyboard and a custom keyboard, so the toolbar doesn't move. The Toolbar shows itself while the editor is focused and a keyboard is up. Pass hidden to control this yourself. The same layout works below a react-navigation header with no changes; see Navigation header.

The layout from the 1.0 docs still works: a React Native KeyboardAvoidingView with behavior="padding", absolutely positioned at the bottom of the screen, around the Toolbar. It needs a keyboardVerticalOffset below a header. On edge-to-edge Android it can leave the toolbar partly behind the keyboard. You can switch to EditorKeyboardAvoidingView without other changes, and it accepts the same absolute style: <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ position: 'absolute', width: '100%', bottom: 0 }} > <Toolbar editor={editor} /> </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>;

You don't need any paddingBottom for the caret. While a keyboard is up, RichText measures how far the keyboard and the toolbar on it reach into the editor. It then keeps the line being typed about one line above the toolbar, also when the keyboard grows (an emoji or suggestion bar), after an image is inserted, after a keyboard switch, and in an editor that ends above the keyboard. See avoidIosKeyboard for the details. Your own toolbar. If you draw your own toolbar on the keyboard, mark it with useKeyboardAccessory so its height is measured exactly. The library's Toolbar does this itself. Other views over the editor. For views that RichText can't measure, such as a floating button over the bottom of the editor, keep extra space below the caret with scrollBottomOffset: const editor = useEditorBridge({ scrollBottomOffset: 60 }); updateScrollThresholdAndMargin still works, but RichText overwrites the value when the keyboard opens or closes. Use scrollBottomOffset for a value that has to stay.
A dynamicHeight editor grows with its content and doesn't scroll itself. Use useScrollToCaret so that your ScrollView keeps the caret above the keyboard. See Editor inside a ScrollView.

Window What happens Edge-to-edge (Expo SDK 53+; targetSdk 35+ on Android 15+) The window never resizes. EditorKeyboardAvoidingView pads for the keyboard and the navigation bar under it. adjustResize (React Native's default without edge-to-edge) The window shrinks for the system keyboard, and EditorKeyboardAvoidingView adds no padding for it. While switching to a custom keyboard, the toolbar can move for a moment; see keeping the toolbar still. adjustNothing / androidKeyboardMode="stable" The keyboard covers the window, as on iOS.

useKeyboard returns whether a keyboard (system or custom) is up, its height, how far it covers the window (keyboardCoverHeight) and where its top is (keyboardTop). Use it to build your own keyboard-aware views.
